newsitem.title: USA: Dole nine points behind Clinton in Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: Dole nine points behind Clinton in Reuters poll.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent

Republican Bob Dole appeared to get a boost from the second presidential debate and trimmed President Bill Clinton's lead to nine percentage points in the Reuters daily tracking poll released on Friday.
Clinton got 43.6 percent in the poll to Dole's 34.6 percent. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot scored 5.8 percent and 13.3 percent said they were still undecided.

The poll, conducted by John Zogby Group International, tracks about 900 likely voters over a three-day period. The latest result, with a 3.3 percentage point margin of error, reflects polling Tuesday through Thursday.
"Dole appears to have gotten a boost from his debate performance and at least achieved the goal of strengthening his Republican base," said pollster John Zogby.

In Thursday's sample, taken after the San Diego debate, the gap between Clinton and Dole was only 5.5 points. However, tracking polls can sometimes show sharp movements because of the relatively small size of the daily sample. Their value lies in monitoring trends over a period of several days.

Despite the seeming connection between Dole's jump and the second debate, however, Clinton won it in the estimation of 41 percent of those who said they had watched. Thirteen percent thought Dole won and 29 percent thought it was a tie.
Dole also briefly closed the gap with Clinton after the first presidential debate on Oct. 6 but Clinton pulled away again a few days later.
Dole has been gaining ground on Clinton for the past four days, cutting the president's lead from over 15 points to the current nine points.
He has been sharply attacking the ethical standards of the Clinton administration.
Even so, over three quarters of Clinton supporters and undecided voters said the attacks would not affect their vote.

Those two groups were asked if their decision would be influenced by the Dole campaign's charge that "the Clinton administration is the most corrupt administration in the 20th century and that if Clinton is re-elected there will be numerous indictments and embarrassments that will put a cloud over the presidency for the next four years."
Only 10.8 percent said this charge would change their vote, while 75.6 percent said it would not.

The Republican nominee seems to have made most of his gains in the South, a Republican stronghold. He has strengthened his position with Protestants and rural voters, among "born again" Christians, among men and among those aged 50 to 64. But he made no gains among political moderates.
Asked which party they would support in their congressional district, 39 percent of respondents said they would vote Democrat and 34 percent for the Republicans.
But narrow pluralities said they would prefer to see the Republicans retain control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives.
